17.steps: 1) Configure IKE Main Mode VPN policies on the central and remote firewalls. 2) Initiate the tunnel by pinging from the central network to a remote VPN host. 3) Make sure that the tunnel is up. 4) Clear the log. 5) Continue to ping through the tunnel. 6) Disable the VPN policy on the central firewall. 7) Make sure that IKE SA and IPSec SA Delete messages are shown on the Log page. 8) Re-enable the VPN policy on the central firewall.
17.title: Main Mode. Re-enable IKE VPN policy with outgoing traffic
17.result: When the VPN policy gets disabled on the central firewall, IKE and IPSec DEL messages are received on the remote firewall. New negotiation doesn't start until the VPN policy on the central firewall gets re-enabled. Then new Main Mode Phase1 and QM Phase2 are negotiated. The log message shows negotiated networks, Crypto Suite, SA life time, and SPIs. Pings from the central network to the remote VPN host are replied.

20.steps: 1) Configure IKE Main Mode VPN policies on the central and remote firewalls. 2) Turn on the check box Enable Windows Networking (NetBIOS) Broadcast in Advanced tab in VPN policies. 3) Go to the Network>IP Helper page in each firewall and turn on the check box Enable IP Helper. Ensure the auto-added entry for the netbios translation is present 4) Ping into the remote VPN host from the host on the local network. Make sure that IKE VPN tunnel is established. 5) On the local host, run nbtstat -a command. On the remote host, capture NetBIOS packets using Wireshark
20.title: Main Mode. NetBIOS through IKE tunnel.
20.result: nbtstat -a command on the local host returns NetBIOS Remote Machine Name Table. EtherPeek on the remote host shows NetBIOS broadcast packet coming from the local host and response packet from the remote host. The response has Source IP address showing the address of the remote host and its computer name. Destination IP address is showing the address of the local host and its computer name. Only the very first time the command is run you will see a broadcast packet, wait until the cache expires to run the command again. NETBIOS unicast packets are sent thru the tunnel irrespective of the enabling the checkbox. Also monitor the netbios bcast traffic that the pc sends out every 3 min. the destination bcast IP address is translated tot he locacl LAN bcast address when the packet gets forwarded on the local LAN.

31.steps: 1) Configure IKE Aggressive Mode VPN policies on the central and remote firewalls. 2) Turn on the check box Enable Windows Networking (NetBIOS) Broadcast in Advanced tab in VPN policies. 3) Go to the Network>IP Helper page in each firewall and turn on the check box Enable IP Helper. Ensure the auto-added netbios entry is created. 4) Ping into the remote VPN host from the host on the local network. Make sure that IKE VPN tunnel is established. 5) On the local host, run nbtstat -a command. On the remote host, capture NetBIOS packets using EtherPeek.
31.title: Aggressive Mode. NetBIOS through IKE tunnel.
31.result:
Nbtstat a remote host computer name> command on the local host returns NetBIOS Remote Machine Name Table. EtherPeek on the remote host shows NetBIOS broadcast packet coming from the local host and response packet from the remote host. The response has Source IP address showing the address of the remote host and its computer name. Destination IP address is showing the address of the local host and its computer name.

Note: nbtstat -a command will only send unicast if the cache entry exists. Make sure cache entry is expired to check the broadcast traffic.
Verify that the destination IP address is translated to the local network directed bcast address whent he bcast netbios request is forwarded on the other side.

35.steps: 1) Configure IKE VPN policies on the central and remote firewalls. 2) On the central firewall, have a more specific VPN destination network (Ex: 192.168.1.0/24) and a super net (Ex: 192.168.0.0/16) in the routing table. 3) Ping into the network on VPN destination from the local host.

35.result: A packet from the local LAN to the destination on the VPN network triggers IKE. The tunnel is established.

45.steps: 1) Create address objects on the local firewall, Local Net (on DMZ zone) and Remote Net (on VPN zone). 2) Configure a VPN policy on the local firewall. Select Local Net as local network and Remote Net as destination network. 3) Repeat steps 1 and 2 on the remote firewall. 4) Ping into the Remote network from a local PC on the LAN subnet. Make sure that IKE doesnt start. 5) Ping into the Remote host from a local PC on the DMZ subnet.
45.title: A tunnel between local network and remote network
45.result: IKE is started by traffic from the local PC on the DMZ subnet to the Remote subnet. The tunnel between subnets is established. Log messages show the completion of negotiation between subnets. The active tunnels are shown on the VPN > Settings page of the local and remote firewalls. Subnets are shown under Local and Remote headers.

48.steps: 1. Configure IKE VPN policies on the central and remote firewalls. 2. Have VPN disabled on the local firewall. 3. Ping from the local host to remote VPN destination. Make sure that negotiation doesn't start. 4. Turn on the check box Enable VPN on the VPN > Settings page on the local firewall and push the Apply button. 5. Ping from the local host into the VPN destination.
48.title: Re-enable VPN
48.result: The log message "VPN enabled by administrator" is generated and printed on the Log > View page. IKE rules are added automatically at WAN > WAN on the Firewall > Access Rules page. Pings from the local host to the VPN destination are replied. IKE negotiation successfully completes.

49.steps: 1) Configure IKE VPN policies on the central and remote firewalls. 2) On the local firewall, set Phase1 and Phase2 SA life time to 180 seconds. 3) On the remote firewall, set Phase1 and Phase2 SA lifetime to 300 seconds. 4) Initiate IKE from the local firewall. 5) Have continuous ping from the local host to the remote VPN host during 5 minutes.
49.title: Initiator's SA life time is smaller
49.result: Phase1 and Phase2 completion log messages on the local and remote firewalls show SA life time = 180 seconds. A new Phase1 and Phase2 will start before 180 seconds will expire.

50.steps: 1) Configure IKE VPN policies on the central and remote firewalls. 2) On the local firewall, set Phase1 and Phase2 SA life time to 300 seconds. 3) On the remote firewall, set Phase1 and Phase2 SA lifetime to 180 seconds. 4) Initiate IKE from the local firewall. 5) Have continuous ping from the local host to the remote VPN host during 5 minutes.
50.title: Initiator's life time is bigger
50.result: When negotiation starts by the local firewall, the remote firewall sends Responder's Lifetime notification message to the local firewall. Phase1 and Phase2 completion log messages on the local and remote firewalls show SA life time = 180 seconds. A new Phase1 and Phase2 will start before 180 seconds will expire.
